title: Hospital headache clinic diaries: two candidate questions, the investigator selects the costing hypothesis over the model's effectiveness pick
notes: Ordinary ambiguity: two candidate questions, and the investigator chooses one at the Hypotheses stage. The need names no design; the single cue 'cost' gives an inferred economic family at create (basis inferred). The retrieved evidence (seven records, one undated and kept null) shows that diary completeness already has a randomised answer, while the costs of the switch do not. The Hypotheses reply offers h1 (completeness, leading towards a comparative study) and h2 (costs and the preventive budget) and selects h1; the investigator selects h2 through the screen (set-field hypotheses.selectedId), which must change the stored selection and flag nothing because no later stage is complete. Questions, Design and the decision follow h2: a cost-consequence analysis with a budget impact estimate, resting on c1 to c4 with both gates met; acceptance is a supported positive and turns the inferred basis into explicit. Claim passages and numbers occur in the cited abstracts; claim c4 carries high uncertainty because it rests on a projection. Record ids were computed by a generator script that loads stableRecordId from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59: normalised-DOI hash for records 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 (ev-0jym8nd, ev-1j6lhsp, ev-0l7s4zc, ev-0mgm1i4, ev-12ochyc) and titleYearKey hash for records 4, 7 (ev-0a92y8p, ev-0zzzcu5, the latter with year null). Requires S11 (inferred basis at create, explicit on acceptance, decision fields), S13 and D5. Catches: an investigator's selection overwritten or lost on reload, an inferred family treated as explicit before acceptance, a guessed year, and a design that ignores the selected hypothesis.

inputs.need:
I am a consultant neurologist in a hospital headache clinic that sees about 1,900 patients with migraine a year. Before each appointment we ask patients to keep a paper headache diary for eight weeks, and the diary drives most treatment decisions: whether preventive treatment is working, whether medication overuse is developing, and whether a patient qualifies for the newer injectable preventives, which need a documented number of headache days. In practice about a third of patients arrive without a usable diary, and appointments are spent reconstructing two months from memory.

A digital diary app is available free to patients through the regional digital health service, and the clinic manager wants to switch everyone to it in January 2027. I am not sure which question to ask first. One route is to test whether the app gives more complete diaries and better treatment decisions than paper. The other is to work out what the switch would cost and save the clinic: nurse time spent setting patients up, shorter appointments, fewer repeat appointments for patients whose eligibility for injectable preventives cannot be judged, and the price of the preventives themselves if more patients qualify.

I need help choosing which question to answer with the time and data I have, how to define a usable diary, and how to make sure that older patients and those without smartphones are not disadvantaged. We have clinic activity data, appointment lengths from the booking system and pharmacy data for preventive prescriptions, and one clinic nurse can give four hours a week.
inputs.constraints: Four hours a week of one clinic nurse from November 2026 to October 2027; existing clinic activity, booking and pharmacy data only; no change to the clinic manager's switch date of January 2027.

The hospital's research office classified an evaluation of the switch as a service evaluation on 2026-09-09 (reference SE-NEU-2026-15).
Injectable migraine preventives are prescribed only after at least eight headache days a month are documented over three months.

records.title: Electronic versus paper headache diaries: completeness and agreement in a randomised crossover study
records.authors: Castellanos-Moyo R, Linde-Achebe T, Park-Oyelaran S
records.abstract: We randomised 164 adults with migraine to keep an electronic diary on a smartphone or a paper diary for eight weeks, then to switch. Days with a complete entry were 91 percent with the electronic diary and 64 percent with paper. Counts of headache days agreed closely when both were complete, but paper diaries were often filled in retrospectively just before appointments. Participants aged over 65 preferred paper more often. The study did not examine treatment decisions or appointment use.

records.title: Headache diaries and eligibility for injectable preventive treatment in specialist clinics
records.abstract: We reviewed 620 consecutive appointments in four specialist headache clinics where eligibility for injectable preventive treatment was being considered. In all, 31 percent of patients arrived without a usable diary. Among them, the eligibility decision was deferred to a further appointment in 58 percent. Deferred decisions added a median of 11 weeks before treatment started. Clinics that sent a diary reminder before the appointment had fewer unusable diaries. The review did not record why diaries were missing or incomplete, and clinics differed in how they defined a usable diary.

records.title: Appointment length and diary availability in a hospital headache clinic
records.abstract: We timed 410 follow-up appointments in a hospital headache clinic. Appointments without a usable diary were 6 minutes longer on average than appointments with one, mostly spent reconstructing headache frequency from memory. Clinicians rated their confidence in treatment decisions lower when no diary was available. The clinic's booked slot length did not change, so longer appointments delayed later patients in the session. The study was done in a single clinic over three months, and the clinicians knew their appointments were being timed.

records.title: Older adults and smartphone health apps in neurology outpatients: use and barriers
records.abstract: We asked 530 neurology outpatients about smartphone use and health apps. Among patients aged 70 or over, 44 percent did not own a smartphone and a further 21 percent owned one but had never installed an app. Barriers included small screens, sight problems and worry about data sharing. Younger patients used health apps widely. The authors recommend that any switch to app-based monitoring keeps a paper option and offers help with setting up. The survey was done in one hospital and may not reflect rural services.

records.title: Budget impact of expanding access to injectable migraine preventives in a regional health service
records.abstract: We estimated the three-year budget impact of injectable migraine preventives for a regional health service. Each additional treated patient cost 4,900 per year in drug costs in local currency. Better documentation of headache days was projected to raise the number of eligible patients by 18 percent, and the budget impact was driven almost entirely by drug costs rather than clinic time. The estimate did not include savings from fewer emergency visits. Uptake assumptions came from a single year of local prescribing data.

records.title: Nurse time needed to set up digital symptom apps for outpatients
records.abstract: We timed nurse-led set-up sessions for a digital symptom app in three outpatient clinics. The median set-up time was 14 minutes per patient, and 22 percent of patients needed a second session. Set-up took longest for patients aged over 75 and for those who needed an interpreter. After set-up, most patients kept using the app for at least three months. Nurse time was not replaced by any reduction in other clinic tasks. The study did not compare app set-up with the time needed to explain a paper diary.

records.title: Headache diary standards for specialist clinics: consensus recommendations
records.abstract: A panel of headache nurses and neurologists agreed minimum standards for headache diaries used in specialist clinics. A usable diary should cover at least 28 consecutive days, record headache days and acute medication days, and be completed prospectively. The panel recommends that clinics offer both paper and electronic diaries and check usability before the appointment. The statement gives no publication date and describes its consensus process only briefly. It suggests that clinics audit the share of patients arriving with a usable diary at least once a year.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A randomised crossover study found electronic diaries far more complete than paper, so completeness has been compared already. Missing diaries lengthen appointments by about 6 minutes and defer eligibility decisions for injectable preventives in over half of affected patients, adding weeks and repeat appointments. App set-up costs nurse time, more for older patients, many of whom lack smartphones. Better documentation may raise the number of patients eligible for injectable preventives, so the largest financial consequence lies in the drug budget.
response.gradeRationale: One small randomised crossover study on completeness; the costing inputs are observational or model-based and from other settings.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five claims; overall certainty low.

response.overview: Cost-consequence analysis of switching a hospital headache clinic from paper to app diaries in January 2027, comparing follow-up appointments from July to December 2026 with January to June 2027, with a three-year budget impact estimate for injectable preventives.

response.summary: Before-after cost-consequence analysis with a separate budget impact estimate.

response.designSummary: Comparison of mean clinic cost per episode between two consecutive periods, with bootstrap intervals; consequences as proportions; budget impact as a deterministic model with scenarios.
response.sampleSize: About 950 episodes per period. With a standard deviation of clinic cost per episode of about 40 (a planning value; the observed value replaces it), the 95 percent interval for the difference in means has a half-width of about 3.6 (40 times the square root of 2/950, times 1.96), small enough to show whether 14 minutes of set-up time for each new app user is offset by 6 shorter minutes per appointment with a usable diary. Usable diaries near 67 percent give an interval of about plus or minus 4.2 points per period.
response.primaryAnalysis: Difference in mean clinic cost per episode with a bootstrap interval from 2,000 resamples; costs at 2026 staff rates.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Usable diaries and time to eligibility decision by period; usable diaries for patients aged 70 or over by diary type; three-year budget impact for injectable preventives under three eligibility scenarios (observed change, half of it, and the 18 percent projection), at 4,900 per treated patient per year (claim c4).
response.missingData: Appointments without booking times are excluded from time costs and counted; missing set-up logs are imputed with the monthly median and flagged.
response.multiplicity: One primary comparison; secondary outcomes and scenarios reported descriptively.
response.software: R; the budget impact model in a documented spreadsheet.
overfittingGuards: Cost items and staff rates fixed before the switch
No subgroup beyond age 70 or over
response.summary: About 950 episodes per period give a half-width of about 3.6 for the cost difference; budget impact by scenario.

response.risks: Minimal: routine data and a change the clinic is making anyway. The risk is to patients who cannot use the app, handled by keeping paper.
response.consent: No individual consent for routine data under the service evaluation classification; app users accept the digital health service's terms separately.
response.data: Pseudonymised extracts; the app export gives completeness by patient study number only (DHS-2026-44).
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: older patients, people with sight problems, people without smartphones and people needing interpreters are least able to use an app; paper stays available, and usable diaries are reported by age and diary type.
response.effectiveness: Shows whether the switch saves clinic time and what it does to the preventive budget.
response.efficiency: Existing data; four nurse hours a week.
response.partnerships: Clinic nurses, the clinic manager, the regional digital health service, the medicines management team and two patient partners with migraine.
response.rebPath: Service evaluation (SE-NEU-2026-15); no research ethics review required.
response.limitations: Before-after design; six months after the switch may not reach steady state.
response.summary: Minimal-risk evaluation with a paper option kept for patients who cannot use the app.

response.partnershipPlan: Two patient partners with migraine, one over 70, review the usable diary definition and the set-up leaflet.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; the clinic's patient feedback from 2026 is summarised.
